items.title: The runtime wars are over... and Node won
items.summary:
Every JetBrains account now comes with a free coding model called Junie Lite. Try it: https://jb.gg/JunieLite

Cloudflare just acquired Deno and the creator of Node.js is finally admitting that reimplementing it was a mistake. Let's dive in.

Want more Fireship?

🗞️ Newsletter: https://bytes.dev
🧠 Courses: https://fireship.dev
items.author: Fireship
items.transcript: Last week, the JavaScript runtime wars officially ended when the guy who put JavaScript on the server and then spent the next decade of toning for it announced that his company, Deno, was joining Cloudflare. And on paper, it looks like a pretty traditional Silicon Valley acquisition where the founder says they're excited for the future, the company says they're excited about the mission, and the employees learn the hard way what a prof stack is. But if you think about it, it's a little weird that a company which already has its own runtime and deployment platform would buy a worse one. In today's video, we'll find out what Cloudflare actually paid for, learn why Ryan Dahl now thinks re-implementing Node was a bad idea, and dive into what the future of Deno looks like now. And spoiler alert, it's not so good. It is October 15th, 2026, and you're watching The Code Report. Back in 2009, Ryan Dahl got on stage at JS Conf EU and introduced the world to a new open-source runtime called Node.js that allowed you to write JavaScript on the server. Nine years later, he went back to that same stage with a talk titled 10 Things I Regret About Node where he spent most of the time tearing apart original project before revealing that he recreated it from scratch, but this time without all the regret. He called it Deno, and unlike Node, it came with its own formatter, linter, and test runner. It supported TypeScript, was secure by default, and had a sensible way to manage external packages. Deno 1.0 launched a few years later in 2020, and by 2021, Ryan announced their serverless platform, Deno Deploy, along with a fresh $5 million seed round. And initially, things were going great. Netlify and Superbase built their edge functions on top of Deno, and Slack used it to power their new app platform. The next year in 2022, they got $21 million in series A funding from Sequoia, launched a web framework called Fresh, and it was looking like they had a real shot at becoming the future of server-side JavaScript. But then, their momentum died. Their biggest problem being that Node didn't just roll over. During those same few years, Node added fetch, a permission model, and the ability to run TypeScript files directly. So, Deno lost its edge. Meanwhile, the products that were supposed to make money weren't gaining enough traction to justify the valuation. A Deno deploy went from 35 regions down to six. Deno KV launched in 2023 and never made it out of beta. And Fresh started going months between releases. At the same time, Ryan took on a legal fight with Oracle over the JavaScript trademark, which Oracle inherited when it bought Sun Microsystems the same year Ryan created Node. It was a noble cause, but a GoFundMe for trademark lawyers probably isn't what Sequoia had in mind when they wrote a $21 million check. The sentiment got bad enough last year that a developer named David Bushell wrote a blog post declaring that Deno was basically dead since every new release was just more Node compatibility fixes in an endless game of catch-up. And ironically, Ryan had come to the same conclusion. He just took a little bit longer to get there. So, earlier this year, the team started to look at hard problems that live outside the runtime like spreading compute across machines, coordinating state, and scaling. The best answer they found was Cloudflare's Durable Objects, which if you're not familiar with, are basically tiny single-threaded servers that each get their own private SQLite database and the ability to hold WebSocket connections. But, the problem with Durable Objects is that they really only work on Cloudflare. So, in August, the Deno team released their own version they called Cell D, which lets you run Durable Objects on your own servers at a fraction of the cost. And surprisingly, Cloudflare was happy to be ripped off like this. In the announcement post, the creator of Cloudflare Workers said that people have accused Cloudflare of using Workers to lock in developers, but the Workers runtime has been open source since 2022 and that they've wanted to build a self-hostable version for years, but just never got around to it. He even admitted he tried building one himself last spring and he couldn't get it to work. So, when the Deno team figured it out with Cell D, Cloudflare did what anyone with a $123 billion market cap would do and they just bought the whole company. The plan is to have Ryan and co-founder Bert Belder merge Cell D into Cloudflare's open source Workers runtime is so that anyone can run workers and durable objects on their own servers with official support from Cloudflare. And because we can't go a whole video without talking about it, Ryan says the big focus is AI agents because durable objects are a natural fit for agents that need cheap compute, persistent state, and real-time connections. But unfortunately, if you're using any Deno product that isn't Cell D, you are screwed. Uh Cloudflare says they'll only continue to ship bug fixes and security patches for Deno for the next year. But after that, they'll stop development altogether. And if you're using Deno Deploy today, you have about 6 months to migrate. So, in the end, with Anthropic acquiring Bun and Cloudflare buying Deno after it bought Vee back in June, the only major JavaScript runtime that isn't owned by a company with a cloud is Node, the one Ryan spent the last 8 years trying to replace. So, if you're one of the Deno developers needing to migrate, you can at least make the move a little cheaper with JetBrains, the sponsor of today's video. Uh thanks to my childhood financial trauma, every time I ask my coding agent to do anything, my brain starts compulsively calculating how many tokens it will cost. So, it's great to see that every JetBrains account now comes with a free baseline model called Juni Light that lives in your IDE and CLI. There's no trial with a countdown clock. It's just a free way to ask questions and get grunt work done without accidentally bankrupting your family. I used it in the Juni CLI on an old side project to rename a bunch of functions and scaffold some tests. And it knocked it all out in a few minutes for $0. I'd still switch to a frontier model for more complex work, which is really easy because Juni Light lives inside JetBrains Air, where you can run multiple agents in parallel and review all their changes before they land. Uh start using Juni Light for free today at the link below. This has been the Code Report. Thanks for watching, and I will see you in the next one.
